svg.text: In the present paper, we pursue

g.text: N1 [Context]
Dataset curation crucial for LLMs
Dataset curation is increasingly crucial for training high-quality
large language models (LLMs).
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Dataset curation is increasingly crucial for training high-quality large language models (LLMs).

g.text: N2 [Prior_Work]
Pretraining data grew 200B → 240T tokens; many selection
methods
As pretraining datasets have grown, from under 200B tokens in 2020
(Raffel et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2020) to 240T tokens today (Li
et al., 2024), it has become critical to identify subsets of the
available data that will lead to the best…
g.title: N2 [Prior_Work] (cites=10) As pretraining datasets have grown, from under 200B tokens in 2020 (Raffel et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2020) to 240T tokens today (Li et al., 2024), it has become critical to identify subsets of the available data that will lead to the best LLMs, and a wide range of methods have arisen to meet these needs (Ilyas et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2023a;b; Engstrom et al., 2024; Everaert & Potts, 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Llama Team, 2024).

g.text: N3 [Limitation]
Data selection methods need expensive retraining
However, data-driven approaches to data selection typically involve
expensive model retraining steps that limit their effectiveness, and no
algorithm has been reported to consistently beat or match hand-crafted
classifiers for data…
g.title: N3 [Limitation] (cites=1) However, data-driven approaches to data selection typically involve expensive model retraining steps that limit their effectiveness, and no algorithm has been reported to consistently beat or match hand-crafted classifiers for data selection (Li et al., 2024).

g.text: N4 [Context]
Can we use existing public LLMs?
Is training new LLMs necessary for data selection? Instead of
training our own models, can we use the growing collection of
publicly available, high-performance LLMs (Wolf et al., 2019;
Beeching et al., 2023) to perform data valuation and…
g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=2) Is training new LLMs necessary for data selection? Instead of training our own models, can we use the growing collection of publicly available, high-performance LLMs (Wolf et al., 2019; Beeching et al., 2023) to perform data valuation and selection?

g.text: N5 [Context]
Benefit: leverage existing $M-spent LLMs
This would have significant benefits: we could leverage the millions of
dollars collectively spent on building these LLMs, and we would have
coverage over a large, heterogeneous collection of high-performance models
varying in size,…
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=0) This would have significant benefits: we could leverage the millions of dollars collectively spent on building these LLMs, and we would have coverage over a large, heterogeneous collection of high-performance models varying in size, architectures, and pretraining data distribution.

g.text: N6 [Context]
Challenge: training data unknown/heterogeneous
Despite these advantages, using existing models for pretraining data
selection is challenging, as the training data for these models are often
unknown and heterogeneous.
g.title: N6 [Context] (cites=0) Despite these advantages, using existing models for pretraining data selection is challenging, as the training data for these models are often unknown and heterogeneous.

g.text: N7 [Method]
Two observable features: loss + benchmark eval
Our key observation is that data selection can be done using two
observable features of all public models today: 1) all open-weight
models produce a causal language modeling loss for a given text,
and 2) all of them can be evaluated on…
g.title: N7 [Method] (cites=0) Our key observation is that data selection can be done using two observable features of all public models today: 1) all open-weight models produce a causal language modeling loss for a given text, and 2) all of them can be evaluated on benchmarks.

g.text: N8 [Prior_Work]
Prior: loss-benchmark relationships shown
Prior work has found systematic relationships between web corpus
loss and benchmark performance (Wei et al., 2022; Huang et al.,
2024), which suggests the possibility of using correlations
between perplexity and benchmark scores as the…
g.title: N8 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) Prior work has found systematic relationships between web corpus loss and benchmark performance (Wei et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2024), which suggests the possibility of using correlations between perplexity and benchmark scores as the basis for a data selection policy.

g.text: N9 [Method]
Select domains via perplexity-benchmark correlation
In the present paper, we pursue this possibility and find a
radically simple approach that is also effective: we select data
via perplexity correlations (Figure 1), where we select data
domains (e.g. wikipedia.org, stackoverflow.com, etc.)…
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=0) In the present paper, we pursue this possibility and find a radically simple approach that is also effective: we select data via perplexity correlations (Figure 1), where we select data domains (e.g. wikipedia.org, stackoverflow.com, etc.) for which LLM log-probabilities are highly correlated with downstream benchmark performance.

g.text: N10 [Method]
Add statistical framework + estimators
To enable our approach, we complement our algorithm with a statistical
framework for correlation-based data selection and derive correlation
estimators that perform well over our heterogeneous collection of LLMs.
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) To enable our approach, we complement our algorithm with a statistical framework for correlation-based data selection and derive correlation estimators that perform well over our heterogeneous collection of LLMs.

g.text: N11 [Result]
Validation on Open LLM Leaderboard
We validate our approach using a collection of pretrained causal LLMs on the
Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard (Beeching et al., 2023) and find that
perplexity correlations are predictive of an LLM's benchmark performance.
g.title: N11 [Result] (cites=1) We validate our approach using a collection of pretrained causal LLMs on the Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard (Beeching et al., 2023) and find that perplexity correlations are predictive of an LLM's benchmark performance.

g.text: N12 [Result]
Relationships enable reliable selection
Importantly, we find that these relationships are robust enough to enable
reliable data selection that targets downstream benchmarks.
g.title: N12 [Result] (cites=0) Importantly, we find that these relationships are robust enough to enable reliable data selection that targets downstream benchmarks.

g.text: N13 [Result]
160M-scale: beats DSIR, matches Li et al. fastText
In controlled pretraining experiments at the 160M parameter scale on eight
benchmarks, our approach strongly outperforms DSIR (Xie et al., 2023b) (a
popular training-free data selection approach based on n-gram statistics)
while generally…
g.title: N13 [Result] (cites=2) In controlled pretraining experiments at the 160M parameter scale on eight benchmarks, our approach strongly outperforms DSIR (Xie et al., 2023b) (a popular training-free data selection approach based on n-gram statistics) while generally matching the performance of the best method validated at scale by Li et al. (the OH-2.5 +ELI5 fastText classifier; Joulin et al. 2016) without any parameter tuning or human curation.

g.text: N14 [Result]
1.4B-scale: beats Li et al. filter on 22-bench agg
In followup experiments at the 160M to 1.4B parameter scale which we
pre-registered, our approach outperforms the best Li et al. filter on the
main benchmark from their paper (an aggregate of 22 benchmarks) when
filtering from their base…
g.title: N14 [Result] (cites=0) In followup experiments at the 160M to 1.4B parameter scale which we pre-registered, our approach outperforms the best Li et al. filter on the main benchmark from their paper (an aggregate of 22 benchmarks) when filtering from their base data pool, and both approaches remain close to each other when filtering from their extensively pre-filtered pool.

g.text: N15 [Result]
Improvement strengthens with scale
We further find that the performance of our approach strengthens with
increasing scale.
g.title: N15 [Result] (cites=0) We further find that the performance of our approach strengthens with increasing scale.
